info.bio:
Moby es un compositor de música electrónica, nacido el 11 de Septiembre de 1965 en Harlem, New York. Luego se mudó a Darien, Conneticut. Su nombre real es Richard Melville Hall y el seudónimo viene de un apodo familiar, que viene de la novela Moby Dick de Herman Melville, su tatara-tatara-tio abuelo.

A Moby se le conoce mejor por singles como "Go", "Porcelain", "South Side" con Gwen Stefani, "We Are All Made of Stars", "Extreme Ways" y "Lift Me Up". También ha publicado música bajo los nombres Voodoo Child, Barracuda, UHF, The Brotherhood, DJ Cake, Lopez, y Brainstorm/Mindstorm.

Moby toca el teclado, la guitarra, el bajo y se mosquea un poco cuando se asume que todo en sus álbumes son samples, solía tocar en una banda punk llamada Vatican Commandos, formada en 1980 pero abandono el punk en 1989 por la música electrónica. Se dio cuenta que sus gustos musicales y su crecimiento como artista iba en una dirección diferente a la de sus bandas anteriores.

Su primer álbum "Moby" incluía el single "Go" que gano popularidad en muchas discotecas y se hizo hueco en las listas del Reino Unido. La canción es tan popular que Moby aun la toca en sus conciertos. "Go" es una pista progressive que usa acordes del "Laura Palmer's Theme" de la serie de TV Twin Peaks

Su primer álbum para Elektra Records fue Everything Is Wrong, que obtuvo buena crítica pero menor éxito commercial. Le siguió un álbum hard rock/electronic llamado Animal Rights en 1996. En 1997, publicó I Like to Score, una colección de música incluida en películas. Entre esas pistas había una versión actualizada del James Bond theme usada en la película de James Bond El Mañana Nunca Muere. Sin embargo, ni Animal Rights ni I Like to Score tuvieron éxito comercial y Moby y Elektra rompieron.

Después de una década de música, el álbum rompedor de Moby fue Play en 1999. Los críticos pusieron muy bien el álbum (publicado en V2 Records) aunque algunos fans estaban decepcionados. El álbum tiene 18 pistas y fue el primer álbum de la historia con todas sus pistas usadas en anuncios: "Porcelain", por ejemplo, apareció en anuncios de TV de Bailey's Irish Cream, Hong Kong's PCCW, Nordstrom, y Volkswagen's MKIV Jetta (en España fue parte de una campaña de TVE1 entre otros); "Find My Baby" estaba en un anuncio de American Express con el golfista Tiger Woods. 

Las pistas del álbum finalmente fueron aceptadas en varios formatos de radio, pero debido a la extensa licencia de Play, podría haber sido un éxito financiero incluso sin aparecer en la radio. Además de la fama ganada a través de los anuncios, Play es también notable por su sampling de viejas grabaciones blues coleccionadas por Alan Lomax. En 2005, Moby teorizó en su sitio Web que este deseo de licenciar su música era resultado de "crecer en la pobreza".

En 2001, Moby fundó el Area:One Festival . Era un festival itinerante que incluía un rango ecléctico de géneros musicales. Una segunda gira fue organizada el siguiente año. 

En 2001 Moby se ganó la ira de Eminem después de catalogar la música de Eminem como misógina y homofóbica. Eminen, después satirizó con Moby (y otros mas) en "Without Me" llamándolo "marica" y cuestionando su relevancia con la reivindicación de que "nadie escucha techno". Moby, replicó que no había tocado techno desde 1992. Los dos tuvieron una confrontación en los MTV Video Music Awards de 2002, aunque Moby expresó su respeto a Eminem como artista.

En 2002, Moby tuvo un breve programa en MTV, Señor Moby's House of Music, que se centraba sobre todo en música electrónica oscura. También en 2002, Moby publicó 18, un álbum de 18 pistas. La canción más popular en el álbum fue "We Are All Made of Stars". Moby dice que escribió "We Are All Made of Stars" por el ataque terrorista del 11 de Septiembre, que sucedió en su cumpleaños.


En 2005 Moby publicó "Lift Me Up", un single de su álbum Hotel, que incluía, además de numerosos remixes, software de Digimpro. El programa permitía a los usuarios remezclar la canción - usando cualquiera de los samples incluidos - y guardarla en MP3. De esta forma, fueron posibles versiones ilimitadas y personalizadas de la pista. Digimpro había utilizado previamente la misma habilidad con el grupo Erasure y su single "Breathe". En lugar de su usual uso de samples, todas las voces e instrumentos en "Hotel" fueron grabados en directo en el estudio por Moby y la vocalista Laura Dawn, Directora Cultural de MoveOn.org.

Para ciertos conciertos de la gira Europea de Moby de 2005, Liveherenow suministró a los asistentes CDs del concierto 10 minutos después de finalizar. Otros artistas de Mute Records como Erasure y Client han utilizado esta compañía para hacer lo mismo.

Moby ha compuesto recientemente la banda sonora para la próxima película de Richard Kelly 'The Southland Tales', aunque está generalmente en contra de componer música para películas, es un gran fan de la anterior película de Kelly 'Donnie Darko' y no pudo resistir la oferta del director.

A parte de la música 

Moby es un vegan, non-denominado Cristiano y auto-proclamado "simpleton" (por sus a menudo valoraciones politicas sinceras e idealistas). Ha expresado su creencia pro-elección. Moby vive en el Little Italy de New York City. Durante una década ha vivido en un pequeño apartamento en un edificio de 5 plantas en la calle de en frente de David Bowie. Hasta hace poco, era copropietario de un pequeño restaurante y cafetería llamado TeaNY, donde ocasionalmente atendía mesas. También organizó el Little Idiot Collective, un grupo de artistas incluye al músico y dibujante James Kochalka.

Activismo

Moby es un bien conocido abogado de una variedad de causas progresivas, trabajando con MoveOn.org y PETA entre otras. Creó el MoveOn Voter Fund's "Bush en 30 segundos" junto con la cantante Laura Dawn y el Director Ejecutivo de MoveOn Eli Pariser.

También participa activamente en activismo independiente. Ha realizado conciertos benéficos para el Instituto para la Función Musical y Neurológica, promoviendo terapia musical. Moby también participa en el Comité de Dirección de Amend.org, una organización sin ánimo de lucro que implementa programas de prevención de lesiones en África.

Es defensor de la red de neutralidad y ha testificado ante el US House comittee debatiendo el tema en 2006

Citas Políticas

    * "Una simple palabra: ugh. ¿Se considera algo una conspiración incluso si lo tenemos justo en frente de nuestras narices?"

    * "Será interesante ver cuáles serán los frutos a largo plazo de nuestra apatía nacional, 'porque hasta ahora han sido bastante malos'"

    * "Estoy realmente algo impresionado por la paciencia de  Iraq  ahora mismo... quiero decir, míralo objetivamente. Han abierto sus puertas a los inspectores de las Naciones Unidas, están siendo bombardeados por las tropas Británicas y Americanas, las fuerzas Americanas están masivamente en sus fronteras, los diplomáticos Americanos están deseando activamente asesinar a Saddam Hussein, etc." . scenes.name: Ambient house e IDM
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Música para relajarse en las «chill-out rooms» que se convierte en género propio, entre el techno y el minimalismo: Chill Out de KLF es su manifiesto; Irresistible Force, Orb (Adventures Beyond The Ultraworld, U.F. Orb: el DJ convertido en compositor clásico), Ultramarine, Global Communication, Spacetime Continuum, Banco De Gaia, Woob. La «Intelligent Dance Music»: Orbital (Brown Album), Eat Static, Sabres Of Paradise, Future Sound Of London, Black Dog, Leftfield, Richard James / Aphex Twin, Plastikman, Moby, Vapourspace. Y la música de baile para no bailarines: Scanner, Faithless, Lo-Fidelity Allstars, Luke Slater, Christian Vogel, David Holmes, Susumu Yokota.

scenes.name: Nueva York: Storm Rave, Joey Beltram y Moby
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: Alrededor de su tienda Groove de Brooklyn, los hermanos Frankie Bones y Adam X organizaron las Storm Rave, con el fanzine Under One Sky de Heather Heart; hacia 1992 la escena incluía a Joey Beltram y Mundo Muzique, que como Second Phase grabaron el himno rave «Mentasm» (1991). En Manhattan, Richard Melville Hall, Moby, despuntó en Instinct con «Mobility» (1990) y su cara B «Go», sobre el tema de Laura de Twin Peaks, número diez británico en 1991 y contrato con Mute y Elektra. Su persona (cristiano, vegano) eclipsó su música, con curiosidades como «Thousand» a mil bpm, hasta que Play (1999), licenciado tema a tema, vendió diez millones.

podcast.title: Fastest Dance Song (1992)
podcast.body: Moby's 1992 track "Thousand" from the B-side of "I Feel It" is in the Guinness Book of World Records as the fastest dance song ever, reaching 1000 beats per minute (BPM). While modern technology allows for compositions up to 15,000 BPM, "Thousand" uniquely achieved a hit single status, reaching number 38 on the British charts, cementing its record. "Moby's Thousand reached number 38 on the British charts."

podcast.title: Industry Disinterest in Play (1997-1998)
podcast.body: Industry professionals and critics, viewing Moby's previous career as a disaster and *Play* as a lengthy, eclectic "brick" of 18 tracks mixing genres like blues, soul, electronic, rave, and instrumental music, often didn't even bother to listen to the album initially. "directamente es que no consiguen ni que lo escuchen."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Initial Rejection by Labels (1997-1998)
podcast.body: After compiling his work for *Play*, Moby sent it to record labels and agents in 1997-1998, but it was rejected without being listened to. The ambient nature of the music was considered out of market trends at the time, and Moby's previous "disastrous trajectory" further fueled industry disinterest. "no consiguen ni que le ganan caso la discográfica."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Delayed Critical Acclaim (2000)
podcast.body: Despite its 1999 release, many positive critical reviews for *Play* did not appear until well into 2000, almost a year later. Critics only took notice and praised the album once its market success, driven by commercial licensing, was undeniable. "muchas en las críticas que tenemos son de muy avanzado en 2000 no bien ni siquiera se habían dignado hacerlo una crítica al disco play de movi hasta que ya estaba muy asentado en el mercado."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Porcelain (Memoirs) (c. 2017)
podcast.body: Moby released his memoirs, titled *Porcelain*, which is described as a very long but personal book. It offers significant insights into the creation and initial struggles of the *Play* album, making it an engaging read for Moby fans and those interested in the early 90s rave scene. "mobi lanzaba sus memorias a las que llamaba porcelain un tocho larguísimo pero súper personal."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: "Four Minutes and 33 Seconds" Cover
podcast.body: Moby participated in a 2019 box set by Mute Records that featured multiple artists covering John Cage's silent piece, "Four Minutes and 33 Seconds." "mute records compiled a bunch of them in a box set featuring... moby..."

podcast.title: "Stealthy Touching" Game Allegation
podcast.body: Moby once claimed to play a peculiar game at crowded celebrity parties, which involved unzipping his pants and "stealthily touching people." He described it as "one of the funniest things you can ever do" and implicated Madonna, Drew Barrymore, Kate Moss, a "known writer," and Dennis Rodman as alleged "victims." Moby has since disavowed these claims, stating they were made as a joke. "Something about unzipping his pants and stealthily touching people. It's a good game and I encourage everyone to play it at some point in your life because it's one of the funniest things you can ever do."

srcs.episode: I Did Not Know That

podcast.title: Animal Rights Activism
podcast.body: Moby is deeply committed to animal rights activism, a cause that inspired his album *Animal Rights*. He frequently uses platforms like Facebook to advocate for veganism, nature conservation, and animal welfare. "movi es una persona muy concienciada en la lucha animalista los que los iráis en facebook vais a ver que está todo el puñete de lo día con rollo esbicanos de naturaleza de salva los cerros y todas estas cosas."

podcast.title: Backmasking in Digital Era
podcast.body: Moby is listed among the artists who have used backward messages, a practice that became more common again with the advent of digital sound editing software in the late 1990s and early 2000s. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Explainer 5

podcast.title: Best-Selling Electronic Album (Years)
podcast.body: For several years, *Play* held the distinction of being the best-selling electronic album in history. "durante años fue el disco electrónico más vendido de la historia."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Bitter Victory: Depression During Peak Success
podcast.body: Despite *Play*'s monumental success, Moby experienced this glorious period poorly. After years of failure, humiliation, and battling depression and alcoholism (as revealed in his book), he found himself in a "very sad psychological state" during the peak of his career, describing it as a "very bitter and sad victory." "el pasa la etapa de mayor gloria y a oje de su carrera en un estado psicológico muy triste es una es una como una victoria muy amarga y muy triste para la para la vida de movi."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Career Collapse (Mid-to-Late 90s)
podcast.body: Following the disastrous reception of *Animal Rights*, Moby hit rock bottom by the mid-to-late 90s. He felt his career had collapsed, believing that his foray into punk had alienated him from the electronic scene and that his career was officially over. "Movi ya asumía que su carrera se había desplomado y que había fracasado."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Career Rescue by Play
podcast.body: *Play* ultimately rescued Moby's career from the failure and industry rejection he had experienced, particularly in an environment that was initially unprepared for his innovative sound. "este disco al final consiguió rescatar a un gran genio que teníamos entra a música del fracaso que le había dado la industria y sobre todo un entorno que no estaba demasiado preparado a lo que le estaba haciendo."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Claims of Inside Information on Trump's Relationship with Russia
podcast.body: Moby has publicly stated his belief that he possesses inside information regarding Donald Trump's relationship with Russia. He asserts that his knowledge comes from an internal source within the CIA. "He claims to have an inside source of the CIA."

podcast.body: Moby participated in a box set featuring "covers" of John Cage's unique avant-garde piece "4 minutes and 33 seconds," which is famously a silent composition. "Depeche Mode, New Order, Moby, a total of fifty artists and all participated."

podcast.body: Moby is among a partial list of artists and bands who have publicly stated that they have been influenced by Joy Division in some way. "You too, arcade fire, smashing pumpkins, nine inch nails, to pesh mode, sisters of mercy, ministry, chain addiction, the smiths, Bjork, Jesus and Marychain, Moby, primal scream, the Charlotains, Interpol, editors, white lies, Frans Ferdinand. I could go on, but I think you get the point."

podcast.title: Dildo Dance Film Appearance
podcast.body: Moby made an appearance in a "weird independent film" where he is depicted dancing with dildos strapped to his head. This unusual cinematic role is noted as something that can be found by those who know where to look. "If you know where to look, you can find Moby appearing in a weird independent film where he dances with some dildos strapped to his head."

srcs.episode: I Did Not Know That

podcast.title: Early 90s Career Struggles
podcast.body: Moby began his career in the early 90s electronic rave/disco scene but struggled to find significant success. Despite releasing some singles that gained some airplay and the album *Everything's Wrong*, he lacked critical acclaim, sales, and recognition, leading him to try different genres like punk. "Movi había comenzado en la escena electrónica un tanto rey un tanto discotequera de primeros de los 90 si mucho éxito."

podcast.title: Eclectic Future Career
podcast.body: After *Play*, Moby continued his eclectic musical path, embracing disco, rock, punk, band-oriented music, and ambient sounds. He was then widely understood as a versatile artist, capable of surprising audiences with diverse offerings, whose work should be approached with an open mind. "movi en el futuro sin entrar a mojor demasiado en el resto de su carrera seguiría haciendo esa parte cléctica que tuvo movi con partes muy discotequeras volvería a hacer rock volvería a hacer punk volvería a tener casi una banda de música volvería a la música ambiental."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Electronic Music Integration
podcast.body: Moby was among the artists who started producing electronic music sounds around the close of the 1990s, as the genre gained widespread attention and influence. "Similarly, electronic music started coming out of Bjork, and Moby, and Underworld, and the Crystal Method, and Daffed Punk, and Air."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Fan Alienation (Animal Rights)
podcast.body: Moby's shift to punk with *Animal Rights* caused him to lose the small fanbase he had begun to build in the electronic/disco scene, as they did not understand the drastic change in musical direction. "los pocos fans que se había conseguido ganar en la escena electrónica no habían entendido el cambio."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Fan of the TR-909
podcast.body: Moby is noted as a long-standing fan of the Roland TR-909 drum machine, a device that, despite its initial commercial failure, significantly impacted music production. "Moby remains a real fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Drum Machine

podcast.title: Financial Success and Millionaire Status (2000s)
podcast.body: By 2000, Moby became a millionaire through *Play*'s success, largely due to the sheer volume of placements in films, ads, and sketches, even though each individual licensing fee was very low. This financial success allowed him to restart and expand his tour, which he had initially cancelled due to the album's poor initial sales. "cuando se ve cuenta movis estaba haciendo millonario gracias a eso y no solo eso sino que tenía que empezar a renovar la gira que prácticamente había suspendido por el escaso es el inicial del play."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Involvement with Trump Administration Claims
podcast.body: Moby claimed in 2017 that the "P-tap" mentioned in the Steele dossier was "100% real." This year, he alleged connecting the son of a deceased Deutsche Bank executive, who possessed documents related to Donald Trump's finances, to Adam Schiff, the chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. These documents were subsequently subpoenaed as part of an impeachment inquiry. "As far back as 2017, he claimed that the so-called P-tap referenced in the Steele dossier is 100% real."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: 60 Mind Blowing Facts in 60 Minutes: The 5th Edition

podcast.title: No Hair as a Statement
podcast.body: Moby is cited as an example of an artist for whom having no hair whatsoever serves as a deliberate and powerful personal statement, on par with a distinctive elaborate hairstyle. "Having no hair at all is just as much of a statement as having a big mullet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: New Rock Hair

podcast.title: Non-Danceable Electronica
podcast.body: Moby was presented as an example of "non-danceable headphone Electronica," differentiating his style from the more club-oriented alternative dance or Electronica acts, focusing on a more introspective listening experience. "Moeby was an example of non-danceable headphone Electronica, not most of his stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 90s Part 7: The Other Genres

podcast.title: One-Man Orchestra Approach
podcast.body: Moby is a multi-instrumentalist, capable of playing over 30 instruments. During the creation of *Play*, he recorded all the music himself in his home studio, layering instruments like drums and other parts, essentially acting as a "one-man orchestra." "el play de movi es movi tocando la batería se graba toca por encima de algo se graba toca por encima algo se graba es él el hombre orquesta prácticamente."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Play - Licensing Strategy and Success
podcast.body: Faced with a lack of support from traditional music outlets, Moby and his manager took the bold step of licensing all 18 songs from his album "Play." This comprehensive licensing strategy led to the album selling 10 million copies and made Moby a household name.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: Post-Play Popularity & Demand
podcast.body: Following *Play*'s success, Moby became a highly sought-after artist. He was courted by magazines that had previously panned his earlier work, with everyone wanting interviews, photos, and collaborations. Artists like David Bowie, Metallica, and Beastie Boys incorporated his sounds, requested remixes, rhythmic bases, and commissioned compositions from him. "todo el mundo quería ir con movi todo el mundo quería hacerse fotos con movi todo el mundo quería hacer entre vistas y artículos de movi."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Prolific & Personal Creative Period (Pre-Play)
podcast.body: After his career collapse, Moby retreated to his home studio, spending two and a half years working through his sadness and emotions by composing music. He created over 100 songs during this period, without a clear intention for commercial release, purely for personal expression. *Play* itself contained 18 of these tracks, and 70-80 more were left unreleased, some appearing on later albums or as B-sides. "compuso más de 100 canciones en esa época en la que sacó el play de hecho el play tiene 18 canciones."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Public Humiliation by Audience
podcast.body: During his punk phase following the *Animal Rights* album, Moby opened for Soundgarden, where audiences threw objects at him and laughed, marking a low point of public humiliation in his career. "movi haría actuaciones como telonero de sound garden por ejemplo en el cual le tiraban cosas al escenario y se reían de él."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Redefining "Selling Out"
podcast.body: Moby is credited with being perhaps most responsible for changing the perception of artists licensing their music for commercial purposes, transforming it from a "giant sin" and career-ending insult into an "essential part of any act's income stream." His success with "Play" demonstrated the financial viability and audience reach possible through sync deals, especially as physical sales dropped by 90% and streaming offered little meaningful income for most musicians. This shift made licensing music an aspirational component of an artist's business plan. "After he showed how there was money to be made from licensing music in an industry where physical media was dying, Mobie changed the concept of selling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 9: (20-11)

podcast.title: Sample Clearance Nightmare
podcast.body: Because Moby recorded *Play* in his home studio without commercial intentions, he used hundreds of samples, rhythms, and loops from various types of music. The process of identifying, licensing, and securing the rights for all these samples became a "nightmare" that took months, leading to some songs being excluded or modified. "recordar todo lo que había hecho movi licenciarlo buscar los derechos y poder trabajarlo fue una pesadilla llevó meses."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Self-Financed Initial Pressing
podcast.body: The label "uv2" eventually agreed to a small initial pressing of *Play*, which Moby largely had to finance himself. "su uv2 se cida a hacer una pequeña tirada que prácticamente acaba pagando movi de su bolsillo."

srcs.episode: MOBY · PLAY. Influencia absoluta de la música de gran consumo

podcast.title: Similar European-American Success Arc
podcast.body: Moby is mentioned as an artist who experienced a similar career trajectory to Sonic Youth, where early success and critical acclaim in Europe significantly influenced and contributed to later recognition and success in America. "Es curioso porque le pasó como a Movy y a otras bandas."

podcast.title: Synth-Heavy Band Example
podcast.body: Listed as one of the new synth-heavy bands emerging in the contemporary music scene. "There's MGMT, there's Owl City, there's Empire of the Sun, Caribou, Phoenix, Beck has been turned onto these sounds, and Moby, check it out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Teany – Vegan Cafe and Online Tea Store
podcast.body: Moby used to own and operate a vegan cafe and online store in New York City called Teany, located at 90 Rivington in Lower Manhattan. Opened in 2002 with his then-girlfriend and partner Kelly Tisdale, the establishment sold 98 different types of loose tea. Despite neither Moby nor Kelly having prior restaurant experience, Moby's financial resources allowed for mistakes, although the business underwent a redesign in 2007. Moby is no longer involved with the restaurant, but Teany Ice Tea is now sold globally, and a book listing Teany tea recipes exists. "Moby used to run a T-shop in New York City called Teeny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
